full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Choudhury, J.—This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and is directed against the concurrent decision of the courts below allowing pre-emption. This rule was issued for examination of the question whether the addition of parties made in compliance with the court's order would be subject to the law of limitation. But this question no more requires examination. The parties in the meanwhile have compromised the case and filed a joint petition of compromise. The question now before us is whether the parties can compromise the case and for the matter of that whether a Civil Revision case may be compromised by the parties. The matter has come to us on reference from a Single Judge of this Court. 

 3. Section 141 of the Civil Procedure Code has made the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits applicable, as far as it can be made applicable in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. The consensus of judicial opinion is that the proceedings" as mentioned in the section refers to original matters in the nature of a suit, such as proceeding in probate, guardianship and so forth and do not include the execution and other proceeding which do not originate in themselves. The proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is in the nature of a suit. The right, title and interest of the transferee vests in the petitioner, if he is successful and as such the order passed in a pre-emption proceeding conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to the land in dispute and as such this is an original proceeding and the determination of the right of the parties are conclusive, whether it is called a decree or an order and the effect is the same. So we feel what provisions of Order 23, rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code would apply in a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act whether it is in the trial court or in the appellate court. 

 4. The next question is whether a revision preferred against the decision of the lower appellate court under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a proceeding. The revisional power as conferred by section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code may be exercised by the High Court either on its own motion or on the application of the parties. If, the High Court suo-moto calls for the record, the question of compromise by the parties does not arise. But the position appears to be different in a Civil Revision case preferred by the parties. There is no provision in the Civil Procedure Code to compel a party to proceed with a revisional application after the issuance of the Rule, if the party chooses not to press the rule and get it discharged for non-prosecution or default. In the absence of any compelling provision in the Civil Procedure Code, there does not appear to be any bar, if the parties by compromise wish not to proceed and have the compromise recorded in the court, if the terms of the compromise are lawful. There is no definition of the word "proceeding' in the Civil Procedure Code "Proceeding" as we understand it to have been used in the Civil Procedure. Code, is a prescribed mode of action for carrying into effect a legal right, it means and includes all the steps and measures for prosecution or defence of an action. A revisional application is a prescribed mode of step in the Civil Procedure Code either in prosecution or in defence of an action and as such the procedure provided for in the Civil Procedure Code shall also apply to civil revision including the provision for compromise on the strength of section 141 of the Civil Procedure Code provided that the revisional application arises out of a suit, appeal or original miscellaneous case or appeal therefrom to which the procedure provided in the Code would apply.
